items.title: Beyond the Dichotomy of Success and Failure: Making Activism Meaningful in South Korea and France
items.affiliation: University of Manchester; London School of Economics and Political Science

extra.summary: ABSTRACT First deployed in the 1970s, prefiguration has recently gained traction among ethnographers of political action as a descriptor for activist practices that foreground participatory democracy, horizontality, and direct action, as seen in social movements like Occupy Wall Street. Notably, ethnographers have come to understand these prefigurative‐inspired, present‐oriented movements as departures from “traditional” social movements, which are often institutionalized via trade unions, associations, and cooperatives, and primarily driven by preestablished, future‐oriented goals. We suggest that this dichotomy, unintentionally reinforced by anthropological scholarship, has a broader analytical implication: It prevents ethnographers from seeing both goal‐oriented and prefigurative practices as equally constitutive of any form of activism. We draw on ethnographies of two seemingly future‐oriented movements typically read as failures: activism led by families bereaved by the Sewŏl Ferry disaster in South Korea and by Esperanto speakers in France. We propose that, while these movements’ long‐term goals remain indefinitely out of reach, their activists have found additional sources of meaning that sustain their long‐term commitment. Understanding activism as a continuous meaning‐making process, rather than a means to an end, would allow ethnographers to understand why such engagements persist. items.title: Four Questions for Ethnographers Under Trumpian Authoritarianism
items.affiliation: University of California, Riverside; Gender Studies

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article examines evolving challenges and ethical dilemmas facing ethnographers working under intensifying authoritarianism in the United States. Because very little of what the United States is experiencing is new, my work here is primarily curatorial in nature, drawing upon the lessons offered by scholars across disciplines in the United States and beyond for whom ethnographic research in authoritarian contexts has always been the norm. Following my recent decision to withdraw a manuscript from publication due to potential repercussions to activist interlocutors, I outline four questions for U.S.‐based ethnographers navigating heightened surveillance, repression, and vulnerability to state violence. These questions focus on (1) how to listen differently in the field and make sense of silence amid eroding public trust, (2) how to look differently and use ethnography to refuse authoritarian chrononormalization of violence, (3) how to question one's own assumptions that exposure via research and publication will necessarily lead to change, and conversely (4) how unexamined refusal to publish may constitute acquiescence in advance. Through this work, I invite scholars to engage in a disciplined hesitation as we rethink the stakes, strategies, and limits of ethnographic work in this political moment.

items.title: The Anthropocene and the End of Nuclear Disaster: Normalizing the Fukushima Nuclear Accident

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article places the concept of disaster in critical dialogue with that of the Anthropocene, which introduces new imaginaries that negatively affect the governance of crises like nuclear accidents. I argue that tropes surrounding the Anthropocene can depict certain events as apocalyptic calamities while also portraying other events as mere “incidents” that do not warrant such labeling. I explore how specific narratives around the Anthropocene legitimize some forms of environmental harm as more important than other threats. This process creates a hierarchization of catastrophes and normalizes certain hazards as less important than others. More specifically, I claim that the very concept of a nuclear catastrophe is at risk of “disappearing” within the Anthropocene. Using ethnographic data based on the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, which happened in Japan, I focus on three popular tropes associated with the Anthropocene that normalize the consequences of nuclear accidents: the figure of the global threat, the disappearance of the idea of pristine nature, and the promotion of resilience and adaptation to new realities. I conclude by reflecting on the broader implications of how Anthropocene discourse shapes which disasters matter and which are relegated to the status of distant, forgettable accidents.

items.title: How Anthropology Can Harm Students During a Genocide
items.affiliation: University of Toronto; Scarborough Health Network; University of Toronto Scarborough

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This essay is about the harm that is committed in the name of care. More specifically, it is about student requests for support during the ongoing genocide in Palestine and an anthropology department's use and weaponization of the language of “care” to do the exact opposite: to cause harm. I examine how the language of care for students and the exception of Palestine are weaponized by administrators—including anthropologists—to silence and shut down conversations about, and support for, Palestine. I demonstrate how the “permission to narrate” stems from certain methods of attention that speak to the university's alignment with settler colonialism, neoliberal capitalism, and anti‐Palestinian racism, even as the university officially acknowledges settler land relations and shares statements about “Diversity, Equity, Inclusion” (DEI). Indeed, such acts of care are often based on the condition that settler‐colonial and capitalist relations remain unchanged—that colonial whiteness remains unchanged—and any attempts to unsettle these liberal, institutional‐settler relations will be met with purposeful occlusion and harm.

items.title: Burying Futures: Artisanal Mining Deaths and the Politics of Negligence in Zimbabwe

extra.summary: ABSTRACT In the gold‐mining town of Kwekwe, central Zimbabwe, injury and death are a constant presence. Collapsing shafts, sudden explosions, gang fights, and neglected health infrastructure characterize the everyday lives of the town's impoverished residents. This article, based on ethnographic research conducted between 2019 and 2023 in Zimbabwe's artisanal and small‐scale mining regions, examines how young miners, their families, and township communities navigate a landscape where untimely deaths and near misses shape political subjectivity and reveal broader modes of state power. By examining how the state and its local enforcers respond to devastation in impoverished communities—and how these communities endure and interpret such recurring losses—the article shows that negligence is not just an absence but an active political repertoire. It contributes to anthropological debates on crisis, necropolitics, and state sovereignty in mineral‐extraction frontiers by showing how authority persists less through outright domination than through calibrated neglect: a mode of rule in which timely intervention is withheld, and the state reemerges selectively during moments of injury, death, or mourning to absorb loss as a political occasion.

items.title: Negotiating Gender and Justice

extra.summary: Long neglected and marginalized by the state, inhabitants of Turkey’s southeast region, particularly its Kurdish communities, look not to the official courts but to renowned local figures, religious leaders, and civil organizations to resolve disputes. This paper explores three types of alternative judicial bodies (AJBs): (1) traditional Heqî AJBs, which prioritize religion and patriarchy in their decision-making; (2) self-identified progressive AJBs run by local civil society organizations; and (3) newly emerging AJBs aligned with state institutions, reflecting the state’s new frontiers in the region. Although these judicial bodies, shaped by diverse adjudicative tendencies and deeply embedded in the region’s religious, political, and social fabric, differ in their impact in terms of whom and what they include or exclude, they collectively provide alternative pathways for dispute resolution. This paper examines the role of AJBs in resolving disputes in the Kurdish southeast, focusing on gender, religious discourses, the involvement of feminist activists and organizations, and the positionality of these bodies within regional politics and sovereignty formation. Based on ethnographic fieldwork in Mardin, it examines interactions between Kurdish AJBs and women’s agency and mobility, while situating AJBs within broader debates on legal pluralism and gender justice in feminist legal scholarship.

items.title: The Diaspora of Pre-Columbian Objects from Atacama into a Global Network of Goods, Collectors, and Museums between 1850 and 1950

extra.summary: Pre-Columbian objects from Atacama not only held value and articulated social relations in pre-European times. To this day, and from at least the nineteenth century onward, they continue to play this role by being exhibited in national and international museum showcases, reproduced in catalogs, or owned by private collectors. It is clear that their past value was changed in these new contexts, but what did not change was their amazing ability to bring individuals and institutions together across time and space, even across continents and generations. The bonds forged in the acquisition, circulation, and possession of these ancient objects and collections formed a global network of relationships between humans and things. Such a web was not woven randomly or whimsically but rather warped within the structure of the world system where the Atacama Desert has participated since the mid-nineteenth century, orchestrated principally by the saltpeter, copper, industrial, and mercantile economies. The circulation and biographies of pre-Columbian objects from Atacama is an extraordinary source for understanding the world system in which they were extracted, exchanged, accumulated, assembled, inherited, and exhibited between 1850 and 1950. This dual reflection also opens up a fantastic possibility to better comprehend the role of the cultural works of the past in the making of each social reality at different moments in time.

items.title: An Archaeology of Redress

extra.summary: Black studies critical theorizations have much to offer the field of archaeology both in theory and in practice. For Saidiya Hartman, redress entails confronting formations of epistemic violence that undergird the archival record; it is a praxis that is always incomplete. This article maps Hartman’s theory of redress onto the practice of community archaeology to explore the opportunities and challenges that arise when archaeologists center youth engagement, capacity building, and cultural and natural heritage stewardship. Using the Estate Little Princess Archaeology Project as a case study, we explore one way archaeologists attempt to offer restitution to the issues their work reveals (i.e., legacies of environmental racism, truncated avenues of economic sustainability, racialized disenfranchisement) through an “archaeology of redress.”

items.title: Staging friendship: towards an anthropology of everyday geopolitics in South Asia
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: This article studies Indian‐Bangladeshi friendship ethnographically, as a contested political imaginary, claim, and relation, from the vantage of its shared borderlands. Staging friendship, I show, is a geopolitical project that engages equally the highest echelons of the Indian and Bangladeshi states and ordinary residents of its marginalized borderlands. In conversation with the anthropological and interdisciplinary scholarship on friendship and the political aesthetics of nationalism, I develop an ethnographic frame to study friendship in and as geopolitics. Zooming in on friendship as political aesthetic and ethical practice allows us to grapple with the hegemonies and hierarchies, the elasticity and the power of such histories, and the everyday practices that constitute the geopolitical as a lively horizon. Moving beyond a traditional conception of geopolitics, this article is an invitation to imagine instead a geopolitics of friendship that centres and takes seriously the difficult work of living solidarity through differences, that many communities are not only engaged in, not as occasional, but as everyday acts of making a liveable world.

items.title: Introduction: On the fickleness of friendship
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: In this Introduction to the special section, I provide a brief overview of the anthropology of friendship, particularly from the 1960s to the present, before focusing on the four articles that form the main body of the section. I argue that anthropologists who do not regard themselves as specialists in friendship will still find much to gain from reflecting on the topic. In addition, I highlight the significance of friendship in pointing to the significance of the fickle in human relations.

items.title: Mandala logic: mytho‐praxis as vernacular political theory in Myanmar
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: This article argues that myth‐making is a form of vernacular social theory, a way of producing conceptual arguments about how social formations work and what is at stake in them. I focus on a myth from Myanmar, the Myth of the Tea Seeds, and its attendant ritual complex, which culminates in an annual religious festival in the highland town of Namhsan. Drawing on the so‐called ‘mandala model’, a classic historiographic approach for the study of Southeast Asia, I show how Ta'ang and Burmese people navigate sedimented trans‐regional power relations, and how highlanders and lowlanders alike engage in acts of retelling, exegesis, and critique that test the limits of the myth as a theoretical tool. What emerges is a picture of core‐periphery politics that looks less like a dialectic of coercion and evasion, and more like a system of antagonistic mutual dependence. Here, mythology is contested ground, a site for interrogating the relationship between abstract social theorization and lived social relations amidst long local histories of accommodation and struggle.

items.title: Knots in the weave: female friendship, ritual tension, and the religious other
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: This article explores the possibility of inter‐religious friendship in a context where the norms of secular citizenship are not necessarily available to form the grounds of community. Hindu and Muslim girls met every day to learn to sew together in a sewing class located inside a Hindu temple compound in a small town in Pakistan. Ritual tensions arose in this space from the shared effort to maintain conviviality across social and theological differences, which were managed through the embodied labour of sewing. Knowledge of the religious other as friend necessitates continually retracing the fuzzy line between intimate familiarity and potential danger. The article argues that the careful management of ritual rivalries and boundaries engendered tenuous forms of friendship grounded in norms of feminine domestic discipline.

items.title: False kings and imagined protestants: why schismogenesis does not explain variation in inequality among Indigenous societies of the Pacific Coast
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute
items.affiliation: University of Washington; University of California, Santa Barbara

extra.summary: Indigenous societies along the temperate Pacific coast of North America embody diverse cultural institutions. This variation is conventionally classified into two distinct cultural areas: the Northwest Coast (NWC) and California (CAL). Discussion of the environmental, material, social, and ideological variation in these societies has a long and continuing history in anthropology. In the last few years, two divergent accounts of this variation have appeared. One, proposed by Wengrow and Graeber, drawing on the concept of schismogenesis – ‘progressive differentiation’ at points of culture contact – posits a sharp contrast between Northwest Coast ‘Fisher‐kings’ and Californian ‘Protestant foragers’. The second views variation across the region as more continuous, focusing on how differential resource control and patron‐client dynamics can generate asymmetries in wealth and power. Our review of Wengrow and Graeber's proposal identifies several flaws: it portrays NWC culture in an over‐simplified and reductive manner, exaggerates the differences between CAL and NWC societies (particularly in the boundary region), and fails to provide convincing evidence that those differences result from oppositional differentiation (schismogenesis). We then explain why we believe opportunities for resource control offer a more empirically valid and theoretically coherent explanation for variation in political economy across these two culture areas.

items.title: The reckoning: ethnographic explorations of the ending of a friendship
items.source: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute

extra.summary: This article examines the ending of a friendship in ethnographic fieldwork. I argue that friendship is a necessarily ambiguous concept and relation, made most distinctive as a ‘friendship’ at its end. Reflecting on a friendship that was ended between this author and an old friend in fieldwork in Halleigh, North Manchester, England, I discuss the friendship's end as a reckoning, a performative act that exposes the structural underbelly of the friendship, as a relation of reciprocity, of obligation, of interdependence, as the history of unspoken material and immaterial exchanges of things, of favours, of time and trust are made explicit and listed, reckoned up, in anger, and, in the present case, when the friendship is being ended. Ethnographically, I address what is exposed about friendship at its ending, the methodological‐cum‐ethical predicaments that the ending of friendships in and after fieldwork may introduce for the ethnographer, and the importance of engaging with and interpreting the breaks and disconnects of the friendship as an ethnographic experience. Examining the reckoning and my own positioning as an anthropologist‐in‐the‐field and friend, I consider more than one form of reckoning at play when re‐engaging with, and writing about, the ending of a friendship.

items.title: Coerced Labor, Caste, and Aspirations for Liberty in Early Nineteenth-Century Bengal: Revisiting the Antislavery Debate from South Asia
items.source: Comparative Studies in Society and History

extra.summary: Abstract This article revisits the debate on the relationship between capitalism and abolition from the perspective of South Asia. It argues that bringing the antislavery debate into conversation with the extensive literature on caste opens up new comparative possibilities. Commercial slavery in the early modern Indian Ocean world is now well established, but global histories of slavery have rarely inspired global histories of antislavery. The dominant interpretation of abolition in South Asia remains focused on the contingent requirements of colonial governance. Through an analysis of legal conflicts over the status of slavery in the eastern Indian province of Bengal in the 1820s and 1830s, I argue that this approach obscures the ethical-political significance of abolition in a context shaped by caste and agrarian slavery. The emancipatory potential of abolition, however, was undermined by a colonial state committed to revenue extraction and social order, as well as by the global capitalist context of counter-revolution. By situating the colonial archive within this wider historical conjuncture, the essay shows how both the possibilities and limits of abolition emerged from the contradictions of liberalism and global capitalism. It thereby puts the South Asian case in conversation with broader histories of revolution and counter-revolution.
extra.journal_query: Comparative Studies in Society and History

items.title: Bourdieusian conception of the state, migrants and radical democracy in the reflexive sociology of Abdelmalek Sayad
items.affiliation: University of Urbino; University of Florence

extra.summary: Abdelmalek Sayad’s sociology of migration can be interpreted as an eminent form of reflexive political sociology and has more than one connection with Bourdieu’s conception of the state as state thought and the sociological-political approach outlined by the French sociologist. Firstly, by placing migrants as the unthought limit of the state, Sayad questions and challenges the classifications of state thought that present it as a homogeneous reality almost ontologically linked to the nation. On the other hand, it will be shown how the restructuring of national political fields around the national/non-national opposition, already noted by Bourdieu in the 1990s, reintroduces the theme of reformulation, in contrast to the current trend, of a radical-democratic approach. Finally, the latter should be able to deconstruct the non-essential link between state and nation from a juridical point of view (as Hans Kelsen pointed out) and thus render the discriminatory prerogatives imprinted in traditional national sovereignty unfounded.

items.title: Middle-class locations: emplacements and displacements of habitus among the French in London
items.affiliation: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

extra.summary: This article examines the alterations of habitus that lead to feelings of emplacement and displacement among middle-class French citizens living in London. I broaden Bourdieu’s concept of split habitus, developed primarily in the context of social mobility, and extend it to questions of geographic mobility. I characterize the French in London as “sideways migrants” who move to a nearby nation with comparable socio-economic indicators and global standing, seeking to maintain their middle-class status through transversal mobility. They are “nation straddlers” who experience dislocations of habitus shaped in the French national social space after relocating to London. I present the cases of four French women in London, drawing upon a larger longitudinal ethnographic study, to expand understandings of how migrant aspirations and practices are connected to the positionality of habitus in both the social space of the nation of origin and that of resettlement. Migration research that situates migrants in national social spaces that they straddle, as in the case of sideways migrants, has important implications for broader questions about the durability and nature of both class and national identity in the contemporary world.

items.title: From Gastfreundschaft to Überfremdung : National Identity and the Origins of Right‐Wing Migration Politics in West Germany, 1973–1983

extra.summary: ABSTRACT This article contributes a historical perspective to scholarship on migration and right‐wing politics in Germany. By examining legal texts, party programmes and parliamentary debates, it traces how West German national identity discourses shaped immigration and foreigner policies between the guest worker recruitment stop in 1973 and the federal elections of 1983. In this crucial but oft‐neglected period, political parties renegotiated national membership criteria amid economic crisis and an emerging multicultural society. Ethnocentric conceptions of German identity by influential right‐wing politicians entrenched an understanding of immigration as a national security threat. After the so‐called refugee crisis of 2015, the far‐right Alternative für Deutschland ( AfD ) mobilised these ideals of ethnic homogeneity in narratives about eroding German sovereignty and citizenship since the guest worker era. The article highlights the importance of analysing such historical constructions and political continuities of the ‘foreigner problem’ to make sense of resurging far‐right politics across Europe today.
topics: German legal, social, and political studies

items.title: Nationalism, Balance of Power, and World Order: Untangling Neorealism's Troubled Relationship With Nationalism

extra.summary: ABSTRACT While many explain the crisis of the liberal international order through nationalism, its treatment by neorealist scholars remains frustrating. Untangling the nationalism–neorealism relationship would help explain the current crisis and enhance neorealism's explanatory power. First, this article reviews and critically assesses neorealist scholarship (defensive, offensive and neoclassical realism) about nationalism. Then, using these insights, I propose a distinctively neorealist theory of nationalism. International power shifts reshape nationalism, which, in turn, conditions the behaviour and discourse of the great powers. Rising material capabilities foster offensive nationalism; diminishing capabilities foster defensive nationalism. Hence, global power shifts—foremost the United States' decline relative to China and Russia—transformed the great powers' nationalism, breaking the post‐Cold War order. This approach enables predictions about nationalism's future. If the global power distribution stabilises, the ‘distribution’ of nationalism should stabilise, too; the evolution of nationalism shows a degree of predictability. Pursuing a ‘neorealist nationalism’ research agenda helps tackle fundamental questions about the international order.

items.title: Epistemic injustice and the Meitei revivalist movement in Manipur, India

extra.summary: Extant scholarship has largely overlooked the epistemic dimensions of the Meiteis’ religious transformation from Sanamahism to Hinduism and the subsequent emergence of Meitei revivalism. In this article, we argue that we can understand both developments better through Miranda Fricker’s framework of epistemic injustice. Fricker conceptualizes epistemic injustice as a form of existential injustice that compromises an individual’s or group’s ‘capacity as a knower’ and undermines their ability to produce knowledge. We use a multi-modal qualitative method that combines initial autoethnographic insights with triangulated secondary sources to argue that the religious transformation of Manipur inflicted epistemic injuries in the form of testimonial injustice and a deeper hermeneutical injury. Finally, we position Meitei revivalism as a consequent project of epistemic recovery, examine its internal challenges, and consider its future in light of Manipur’s extant politics.

items.title: Infrastructure nationalism and sovereignty by settlement in Tibet: The case of xiaokang border villages

extra.summary: This article critically examines China’s Xiaokang Border Village Programme (2017–20) in the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), situating it within Xi Jinping’s broader strategy of ‘governing the borders to govern the country’. Ostensibly framed as a poverty alleviation and rural revitalization initiative, the programme mobilized billions in state funding to construct or rebuild more than 600 model villages in Tibet’s border counties. Drawing on a range of new sources, the article argues that these villages are less developmental tools than instruments of territorial consolidation, securitization, and ideological transformation. By reconfiguring spatial relations, relocating border populations, and embedding Han-led Chinese Communist Party (CCP) institutions, these xiaokang villages function as micro-sites of infrastructure nationalism and colonial-style governance, inscribing Han norms into Indigenous landscapes and subjectivities to further CCP control over once autonomous communities in the farthest reaches of the People’s Republic of China.

items.title: A culturally tailored Zhuang embroidery intervention for psychological well-being among Zhuang adults in the retirement transition in Guangxi: a waitlist-controlled quasi-experimental study

extra.summary: Background Arts- and craft-based community programs may support psychological well-being in later life, yet few studies have examined culturally tailored ethnic heritage crafts as public health interventions in their communities of origin. Methods This waitlist-controlled quasi-experimental study evaluated an eight-week intervention integrating Zhuang embroidery practice, cultural storytelling, and group exchange among community-dwelling Zhuang adults aged 55–65 years in Guangxi, China. Eighty participants were allocated by community cluster to intervention or waitlist control groups and assessed at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and 12-week follow-up. Psychological well-being was the primary outcome; loneliness, social connectedness, general well-being, ethnic identity, process perception, and qualitative interview findings were secondary or exploratory materials. Results The intervention group showed greater immediate improvement in Ryff psychological well-being than waitlist controls. Baseline-adjusted sensitivity analysis supported the immediate Ryff signal, whereas the follow-up difference was attenuated. Secondary outcomes were less consistent: WEMWBS and loneliness showed short-term favorable movement, whereas social connectedness, WHO-5, and ethnic identity findings were weaker or exploratory. items.title: Can Intangible Cultural Heritage Resources Stimulate Regional Entrepreneurial Activity?—Empirical Evidence from the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region
items.affiliation: Nanning Normal University; Fujian Normal University; Universiti Putra Malaysia; Northern University of Malaysia

extra.summary: In line with the world’s goals of sustainable development, cultural resources are now being used to promote both cultural inheritance and regional economic revitalisation. This paper studies whether intangible cultural heritage (ICH) resources can promote regional entrepreneurial activity by analyzing panel data from 14 prefecture-level cities in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China, from 2007 to 2023. The empirical results indicate that ICH resources significantly promote entrepreneurial activity in Guangxi; specifically, both the stock of ICH projects and the stock of inheritors show significantly positive effects, and the findings remain robust after a series of tests. The results suggest that ICH can be used to carry cultural values and serve as a resource for place-based development that supports entrepreneurship through heritage commercialisation, cultural consumption and local industrial integration. This study incorporates ICH into the regional entrepreneurship analysis framework, providing new empirical evidence for the economic value of cultural heritage and its role in innovation-driven development.

items.title: Prevalence and associated factors of functional disability among middle-aged and older adults: evidence from 12 ethnic groups in Yunnan, China
items.source: International Journal for Equity in Health

extra.summary: Functional disability is a growing public health concern in aging populations worldwide, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. In China, rapid population aging and substantial ethnic and cultural diversity further complicate this issue, yet evidence focusing on functional disability among ethnic minority groups remains limited and overlooks intragroup heterogeneity. Thus, this study aims to investigate the prevalence and determinants of functional disability among middle-aged and older adults across different ethnic groups in a multi-ethnic setting. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 5,180 middle-aged and older adults from 12 ethnic groups in Yunnan. Sociodemographic characteristics and health conditions were collected through structured questionnaires. Functional disability was assessed using the functional assessment framework, comprising Physical Self-Maintenance Scale (PSMS) and Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL) scale. Standardized prevalence rates for the 11 minority ethnic groups were calculated using the age distribution of the Han population as the standard. Multivariable logistic regression were applied to identify factors associated with functional disability, with results reported as odds ratios ( OR ) and 95% confidence intervals ( 95%CI ). items.title: Tripartite Evolutionary Game and Simulation Analysis of Regulating Service Value Realization: A Case Study of Yunnan Province, China

extra.summary: The sustainable provision of regulating services—such as climate regulation, water purification, and soil conservation—is fundamental to both ecological integrity and human well-being, yet the market mechanisms required to sustain their value remain critically underdeveloped. To explore the sustainable process of realizing the value of regulating services, this study introduces three stakeholders—environmental protection enterprises, the government, and residents—and constructs an evolutionary game model to analyze the behavioral decisions of each stakeholder and the key factors influencing system equilibrium. To validate the theoretical model, we further employed MATLAB R2023a to conduct simulation analyses using a real-world case study and data from Yunnan Province, examining the impact of various variables on the outcomes of the evolutionary game. The following results were obtained: (1) Multiple equilibrium solutions exist within the evolutionary game system, indicating that there is no single path to realizing the value of regulating services. Among these, full government support is key to realizing the value of regulating services. (2) A critical parameter exists in the multi-party game for realizing the value of regulating services, and this parameter exhibits a significant threshold effect; once the threshold is exceeded, the behavioral decisions of the participating actors will change. items.title: A Century of Population Dynamics in Arid Xinjiang, China: County-Level Change, Demographic Structure, and Spatial Patterns, 1909–2020
items.affiliation: Northwest Normal University; Shaanxi Normal University

extra.summary: Reconstructing long-term population dynamics contributes to understanding the processes underlying the formation of present-day population patterns and provides a historical perspective for addressing future demographic challenges. This study reconstructs county-level population changes in Xinjiang, China, from 1909 to 2020 by integrating historical population records with modern census data and applying historical demographic methods and GIS-based spatial analysis. The results show that Xinjiang’s population increased nearly twelvefold over the past century, with two major decline periods in the 1930s and early 1960s. Significant demographic changes included declining household size, a more balanced sex ratio, and limited population aging. Spatially, northern Xinjiang exhibits a concentrated population pattern closely associated with urbanization, transportation infrastructure and policy incentives, while southern Xinjiang’s population is more dispersed following a linear distribution along oases. This study provides a long-term perspective on population evolution in arid regions and highlights the value of incorporating historical demographic dynamics into land and water resource management.

items.title: Coupling Mechanism and Driving Paths of the Spatial Differentiation of Tourism Attractions from the Perspective of Tourist Perception—A Case Study of Xinjiang, China
items.affiliation: Xinjiang University; Guangdong-Hongkong-Macau Joint Laboratory of Collaborative Innovation for Environmental Quality; Guangzhou Urban Planning Survey & Design Institute; Sun Yat-sen University

extra.summary: As the culture and tourism industry moves toward high-quality development, tourist perception has become a core dimension for measuring that quality. Most existing work on tourism spatial differentiation still looks at the supply side, and describes the pattern of tourism attractions. It pays limited attention to how supply and demand couple with each other, and it offers little systematic evidence from large-scale, highly heterogeneous regions. This study combines multi-source tourism point data with review texts from Trip.com (hereafter, Trip) and Rednote (Xiaohongshu). Using RoBERTa-wwm, a pretrained Chinese language model with whole-word masking, together with a coupling-coordination model and the geographical detector, we analyze how the spatial differentiation of tourism attractions couples with tourist perception, and we trace the driving mechanism to land resources, tourism resources and socioeconomic conditions. The results show that tourist sentiment perception in Xinjiang forms a spatial pattern that is led by core cities and declines outward layer by layer, and the coupling coordination between the distribution of tourism attractions and tourist sentiment perception remains higher in the north and lower in the south. The two systems do not, however, follow a simple linear relation: infrastructure coverage emerges as the strongest correlate of coordination, whereas regional economy and population size explain it only weakly. items.title: Borderland extraterritoriality: The Yunnan-Burma frontier meetings (1902–1949)
items.affiliation: East China University of Political Science and Law

extra.summary: Abstract Britain exercised a distinctive form of extraterritorial jurisdiction around the Yunnan-Burma border before 1949. In 1902, Chinese and British officials established a joint trial system under the 1902 Manai Agreement. From then on, Chinese, British, and Burmese officials convened temporary frontier meetings each winter in border areas, including in Manai, Nawngma, and Sima. These meetings adjudicated disputes involving theft, injuries, and trans-frontier cultivation pursuant to tribal customary law. The frontier meetings normally issued four distinct types of judgments and awarded a uniform remedy in the form of damages. This system served the practical needs of border tribes by delivering swift justice to prevent blood feuds and maintain law and order. These meetings developed a case law for resolving borderland cases that diverged from the national laws of both China and Britain. This system was jointly administered by Chinese, British, and Burmese officials under ostensibly reciprocal terms, though Britain’s exercise of extraterritorial jurisdiction in China ultimately placed a heavier burden on the Chinese side. The joint trial system came to an end after Burma officially gained independence in 1948. British extraterritorial jurisdiction in China was not absolute but operated through distinct jurisdictional systems in the interior and in the borderlands.

items.title: Infrastructure nationalism and sovereignty by settlement in Tibet: The case of xiaokang border villages

extra.summary: This article critically examines China’s Xiaokang Border Village Programme (2017–20) in the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR), situating it within Xi Jinping’s broader strategy of ‘governing the borders to govern the country’. Ostensibly framed as a poverty alleviation and rural revitalization initiative, the programme mobilized billions in state funding to construct or rebuild more than 600 model villages in Tibet’s border counties. Drawing on a range of new sources, the article argues that these villages are less developmental tools than instruments of territorial consolidation, securitization, and ideological transformation. items.title: Built Heritage Perception and Spatial Patterns of Tourist Affect in Dali Bai Autonomous Prefecture, China: A Social Media–Based Assessment
items.affiliation: Ningbo University; Huazhong University of Science and Technology

extra.summary: Against the backdrop of the concurrent processes of tourism development, spatial commercialisation, and architectural heritage conservation, identifying tourists’ cognitive images of destinations and differences in textual valence provides an important basis for evaluating the quality of tourism built environments and implementing fine-grained spatial governance. Taking Dali Bai Autonomous Prefecture in Yunnan Province as the study area, this study analyses 32,992 Ctrip attraction reviews using high-frequency term identification, two-level theoretical coding, a semantic co-occurrence network, and affective analysis to construct an attraction-level image-affect analytical framework. The results show that, under a theory-guided codebook, review content can be organised into four dimensions: natural landscapes, built heritage, ethnic culture, and services and accessibility. Natural mountain–lake scenery has the broadest review coverage, while strong semantic associations among architectural character, Bai vernacular dwellings, and Bai culture indicate that built heritage is an important spatial representation through which tourists recognise local culture. Textual valence is predominantly positive: positive, neutral, and negative affective terms account for 71.87%, 22.65%, and 5.48%, respectively. Positively coded propositions mainly concern natural and ecological landscapes, accounting for 44.12%, whereas 71.92% of negatively coded propositions concern services and accessibilit

items.title: Multi-dimensional impacts of rural tourism on poverty in China’s post-poverty era: a sustainable livelihoods approach

extra.summary: After China declared victory over absolute poverty in 2020, the question shifted from whether tourism can reduce poverty to whether the livelihoods it built can last. This study uses the Sustainable Livelihoods Approach to examine that question, drawing on 29 semi-structured interviews in Jianchuan County, Yunnan. The findings show that tourism sets two processes in motion at once: the restructuring of material assets and the building of residents’ capabilities. These run in parallel, each reinforcing the other. When both are sustained, a further shift appears: restored dignity, renewed hope, and stronger community cohesion. Yet spatial unevenness, profit leakage, price inflation, and seasonality limit how widely these benefits reach. Theoretically, the study empirically specifies how the SLA operates under post-poverty conditions by tracing capitals’ interaction. Practically, it calls for post-poverty monitoring that looks beyond income, sustained investment in capability-building, and diversification strategies to buffer seasonal and distributional risks.

items.title: Contesting Collecting: Indigenous Material Cultures

extra.summary: This dialogue explores how we understand and contest the collecting of Indigenous material cultures.Poskett, using several case studies explores how Indigenous and non-Indigenous perspectives can complicate fixed notions of materiality.Russell, drawing on her own heritage and interdisciplinary research, emphasizes crosscontextualization and the agency of Indigenous communities in shaping how cultural materials are interpreted.Together, they ask how Indigenous and non-Indigenous perspectives can reshape the history of science and museums.
